nodes.name: Arithmetic combinations of functions
nodes.description: Build functions by adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing the outputs of simpler functions at the same input. Use common input domains and exclude zero divisors. Construct and interpret contextual models from standard function types; distinguish these operations from composition.
criteria: Form and evaluate arithmetic combinations from formulas, tables, or graphs at matching inputs, retaining the common domain and any divisor restrictions.
Construct a contextual function from simpler standard types, such as a constant plus a decaying exponential, and explain what each component and the combined output represent.

nodes.name: Eventual exponential growth beyond polynomial growth
nodes.description: For a positive exponential growth model \(A b^x\), with \(A>0\) and \(b>1\), compare values with a fixed increasing polynomial growth model as \(x\) increases. Use graphs and tables to observe eventual dominance over linear, quadratic, and higher polynomial growth, including bases close to one.
criteria: Extend tables and adjust graph windows to compare exponential growth with linear, quadratic, and higher polynomial models on a sufficiently large input range.

Describe the eventual exponential dominance observed in sufficiently extended graphs and tables, recognizing that a short table or a small graph window can hide that behavior. A formal asymptotic proof is not required.

nodes.name: Partitioning a directed segment in a given ratio
nodes.description: For distinct coordinate points \(A,B\) and a positive ratio \(AP:PB=m:n\), find the internal point \(P=A+\frac{m}{m+n}(B-A)\). The fraction is measured from the first named endpoint; reversing the direction changes which fraction is used. Scope is internal division, not external division.
criteria: Convert a part-to-part ratio into the fraction of the displacement from the starting endpoint, and compute both coordinates, including horizontal and vertical segments.
Check that the point lies between the endpoints and has the required ratio; explain the midpoint case and the effect of reversing the directed segment.

nodes.name: Modeling with area and volume densities
nodes.description: Use quantity per positive unit area or volume to model populations, mass, energy, or counts. Relate density, total quantity, and geometric measure with consistent units. Identify the region or solid and assess any uniform-density and shape approximations used in the estimate.
criteria: Form and interpret densities based on area and volume, choosing compatible square or cubic units and distinguishing density from total quantity.
Use a geometric model to estimate density, total quantity, area, or volume, or compare such models; state assumptions and report precision appropriate to the available information.

nodes.name: Deriving the sine formula for triangle area
nodes.description: For adjacent sides \(a,b>0\) and included angle \(0<C<\pi\) in a nondegenerate triangle, derive \(K=\tfrac12 ab\sin C\) by constructing an altitude and substituting its trigonometric expression into the base-height formula. Account for right and obtuse configurations.
criteria: Draw the altitude to the line containing the chosen base and express its length using a right triangle. When the included angle is obtuse, use the equality of the sines of supplementary angles.
Substitute the height into the base-height area formula to derive the general included-angle formula, explain the right-angle case, and use matched sides and included angle in area calculations.

nodes.name: Complex solutions of real quadratic equations
nodes.description: Solve \(ax^2+bx+c=0\) with real coefficients, \(a\ne0\), and \(b^2-4ac<0\). Extend completing the square or the quadratic formula using \(i^2=-1\), obtaining both nonreal conjugate solutions in rectangular form. A negative discriminant excludes real roots, not complex roots.
criteria: Use completing the square or the quadratic formula to obtain both roots, simplifying a negative real radicand with the imaginary unit and retaining the plus-minus pair.
Verify the two solutions in the equation or its equivalent completed-square form, and distinguish no real solution from no solution in the complex numbers.

nodes.name: Rational closure and irrationality under arithmetic
nodes.description: Use integer-fraction representations to justify rational closure under addition and multiplication, and use reverse arithmetic to show that adding a rational to an irrational or multiplying an irrational by a nonzero rational gives an irrational. Justify rational additive inverses and reciprocals of nonzero rationals for these reverse arguments, preserving the nonzero condition.
criteria: Represent a rational number as an integer numerator over a nonzero integer denominator, including an integer over one. Explain why sums and products retain this form; show that negation preserves it and that a nonzero rational has a rational reciprocal.

Give general arguments for the rational-plus-irrational and nonzero-rational-times-irrational cases using the rational closure and inverse facts to justify reverse subtraction or division. In the product argument, divide only by the nonzero rational multiplier. Explain the zero-factor exception and why the conclusions do not extend to two irrational inputs.

edges.scope: Constructing a contextual function as a constant plus a varying quantity.
edges.rationale: The existing topic's spring diagnostic constructs L=10+0.5m from an initial length and extension per unit mass. This prepares interpreting the two components of a contextual arithmetic combination, without covering general combinations of standard function types.

edges.scope: Combining outputs of functions at the same input on their common domain.
edges.rationale: Pointwise arithmetic presupposes that each component assigns one output to an allowed input; that input-output meaning and domain are explicit in the existing function concept.

edges.scope: Formula-based combinations that inherit denominator or even-root restrictions.
edges.rationale: The existing domain topic finds conditions that make each component formula meaningful. This prepares retaining those restrictions and excluding zero divisors in an arithmetic combination; the common-domain rule itself is taught in the new topic.

edges.scope: Graph and table methods for constructing the sum in IM task 230.
edges.rationale: Reading component values from graphs or tables directly prepares the matching-input calculation. Formula-based combinations can be learned without that particular representation.

edges.scope: Understanding and evaluating the exponential component with base greater than one.
edges.rationale: The comparison explicitly concerns exponential values as input increases. The existing definition supplies the exponential family and its evaluation, but does not contain eventual comparison with polynomials.

edges.scope: Observing and comparing function outputs through tables and graphs.
edges.rationale: The target observation uses both representations, so reading their input-output values is a direct component rather than a general prerequisite imported from the coherence map.

edges.scope: Locating and checking an internal division point in the coordinate plane.
edges.rationale: Interpreting both endpoint coordinates and the resulting point is intrinsic to the coordinate partition procedure.

edges.scope: Turning a part-to-part ratio into a fraction of a whole segment.
edges.rationale: Dividing a total quantity in a given ratio directly prepares the conversion from m:n to m/(m+n). It does not itself locate a point or specify the starting endpoint.

edges.scope: Vector derivation using a scaled endpoint displacement.
edges.rationale: Coordinate vector subtraction, scaling, and addition support the displayed affine expression. Students can instead compute coordinate changes directly, so vector formalism is not required.

edges.scope: Interpreting quantity divided by area or volume as a per-unit measure.
edges.rationale: The existing ratio concept supplies quotient meaning, which directly supports density. It omits area/volume denominators, derived units, and geometric modeling assumptions.

edges.scope: The spherical-cell volume calculation in IM task 1146, not every density model.
edges.rationale: The linked cell-count estimate obtains cell volume from its radius before applying mass density. Other density problems provide the geometric measure or use other shapes, so sphere volume is a method-specific preparation.

edges.scope: Substituting a trigonometric height into the base-height area formula.
edges.rationale: The derivation explicitly starts with one half of base times perpendicular height; computing an area by an unrelated formula would not meet this derivation.

edges.scope: Constructing and interpreting the auxiliary perpendicular, including an extended side.
edges.rationale: The native standard specifies an altitude construction. The existing altitude topic defines that perpendicular and covers acute, right, and obtuse configurations.

edges.scope: Expressing the altitude as a side length times an acute-angle sine.
edges.rationale: The right-triangle sine ratio is the direct mathematical step connecting the auxiliary height with a side and angle.

edges.scope: The obtuse-included-angle branch of the specified altitude derivation, replacing the sine of the supplementary acute angle by the sine of the included angle.
edges.rationale: This branch explicitly uses the supplementary-angle sine identity to convert the right-triangle height expression into the stated included-angle formula. The requirement is scoped to this identity in the obtuse branch, not to every reduction formula or every triangle-area method.

edges.scope: Interpreting nonreal roots using the imaginary unit and rectangular complex form.
edges.rationale: Writing the roots as real part plus imaginary part uses the existing complex-number definition and i squared equals minus one. Arithmetic skill alone does not assert that the equation has been solved.

edges.scope: The completed-square solution method in IM task 1690.
edges.rationale: Converting the equation to a square equals a constant is the immediate algebraic step in that method. The quadratic formula offers another route, so completing the square is not a universal prerequisite of the new topic.

edges.scope: Extending the familiar real quadratic formula to a negative discriminant.
edges.rationale: The existing formula topic explicitly assumes a nonnegative discriminant. Its algebraic pattern prepares the extension, but it cannot be aligned as solving nonreal roots.

edges.scope: Recognizing integers and fractions as rational numbers before developing integer-fraction representations.
edges.rationale: The existing topic defines rational numbers as integers and fractions. The new topic explicitly develops the integer-over-integer representation, including integers over one, and supplies the closure and inverse arguments; those arguments are not attributed to the existing classification topic.

edges.scope: Distinguishing irrational real values from rational values.
edges.rationale: The mixed-input claims require the rational/irrational distinction. The new topic connects the existing decimal characterization to not having an integer-fraction representation and proves behavior under arithmetic.

reviews.coverageReason: Added general arithmetic operations on function outputs and contextual construction from standard function types. Existing cnm_199 already constructs a spring model as L=10+0.5m, a contextual sum of a constant and a proportional function, and requires interpreting the contextual domain. That is genuine partial coverage, but it does not explicitly develop general arithmetic combinations across function types or representations. Composition and differentiation of sums are different tasks. The linked graph-addition task is expressly preparatory, so its success alone does not establish the full standard. The new topic separately requires constructing and interpreting a contextual combination.

sources.note: F-BF.A.1b requires arithmetic combination in the function-building modeling cluster, distinct from composition in 1c.
Task 230 omits formulas to examine pointwise graph addition. Its commentary explicitly describes this as preparation for contextual construction; the example is not a complete assessment of 1b.
Functions Progression, printed page 12, builds a cooling model from ambient temperature plus an exponentially decaying temperature difference.

alignments.reason: Includes arithmetic construction and interpretation of models from standard function types. It also explicitly handles representation-based arithmetic, common domains, and zero-divisor restrictions; the native example alone addresses addition.

reviews.coverageReason: Added eventual exponential-versus-polynomial comparison using tables and graphs. Distinguishing model families, exponential monotonicity, geometric-sequence growth, and polynomial tail signs do not explicitly establish this cross-family conclusion. Task 368 supplies a delayed linear crossover example; the native standard additionally requires quadratic and general polynomial growth, which are explicit in the new topic without requiring calculus or a formal asymptotic proof.

sources.note: F-LE.A.3 explicitly includes linear, quadratic, and general polynomial comparators and specifies observation with graphs and tables.
Task 368 contrasts a base just above one with a linear function. Continuing the initially misleading table reveals the eventual crossover.
Task 367 compares exponential and cubic growth directly. Students extend a table that initially favors the cubic and explain how the two growth factors behave for larger inputs.

alignments.reason: Directly observes and describes eventual dominance of positive exponential growth over linear, quadratic, and fixed polynomial growth through graphs and tables, without requiring a formal asymptotic proof. The positivity and base-greater-than-one conditions make explicit the native growth premise.

reviews.coverageReason: Added internal directed-segment division, often called the section formula. Scalar vector operations and dividing a total in a ratio provide methods and preparation, but neither explicitly locates the ratio point from ordered endpoints. The new procedure covers positive internal ratios in both coordinates, including reversal of direction; no external-division requirement is inferred from the word directed.

sources.note: G-GPE.B.6 specifies a point between two given endpoints on a directed segment and a given partition ratio.
Task 1867 computes points one-third from one endpoint and two-thirds from the other by scaling coordinate changes; its commentary identifies segment division as the target.

alignments.reason: Computes and checks the internal point in a specified ratio from the directed starting endpoint, for arbitrary distinct coordinate endpoints. External division is outside both recorded scopes.

reviews.coverageReason: Added area and volume density modeling, rather than equating density with a geometric formula or a generic ratio. The cell example uses mass per volume, whereas the standard also covers quantities per area and other volume-based quantities. The new topic explicitly includes both kinds of denominator, consistent derived units, and the modeling assumptions needed to turn a geometric measure into an estimate.

sources.note: G-MG.A.2 includes both area-based and volume-based densities in modeling, with population and energy examples.

Task 1146, also aligned by IM to G-MG.A.2, combines spherical volume, mass density, and total body mass. Its commentary discusses approximation assumptions and suitable reporting precision, not a verified biological cell count.
Geometry Progression, printed page 19, connects density with geometric modeling and rough Fermi estimates under simplifying assumptions.

alignments.reason: Covers applying densities based on both area and volume in modeling and additionally makes unit consistency, uniformity assumptions, and appropriate approximation precision explicit.

reviews.coverageReason: Added the missing altitude-based derivation of the general sine-area formula. The Chinese descriptions of cnm_h092 and cnm_h093 cover sine-law computations and selecting sine/cosine laws for unknown sides or angles, not sine-area derivation. The base-height area and altitude topics contain necessary components; area-radius identities and Heron's formula are distinct results. IM task 1322 supplies a useful equilateral altitude example but cannot justify a complete-standard mapping: IM itself tags it G-CO.C.10 and G-SRT.C, and it does not derive the general formula. The new topic requires that derivation with acute, right, and obtuse cases.

sources.note: G-SRT.D.9 requires deriving the included-angle sine-area formula by an auxiliary perpendicular, rather than merely applying a known formula.

Task 1322 uses an altitude and acute-angle sine to calculate one equilateral triangle's area. Its current IM alignments do not include G-SRT.D.9; treat it as a supporting example, not full derivation evidence.

alignments.reason: Explicitly derives the formula through the required auxiliary perpendicular for general nondegenerate triangles, and additionally requires using the resulting formula for numerical area calculations.

reviews.coverageReason: Added solution of real-coefficient quadratics with negative discriminant. cnm_222 explicitly restricts its formula method to nonnegative discriminants; cnm_223 only says a negative discriminant gives no real roots. Complex arithmetic, conjugate-root symmetry, and the fundamental theorem of algebra do not explicitly supply this solution procedure. Task 1690 confirms that completing the square must continue past a negative radicand to obtain both nonreal roots.

sources.note: N-CN.C.7 requires solving quadratics with real coefficients and complex solutions, distinct from complex arithmetic and root-existence statements.
Task 1690 completes the square for two negative-discriminant quadratics. Its commentary also derives the general quadratic formula with a nonzero leading coefficient.
Number Progression, printed page 18, explains that the imaginary unit allows the quadratic formula to continue when its discriminant is negative.

alignments.reason: Solves the intended nonreal-root case for arbitrary real quadratic coefficients, with nonzero leading coefficient, both conjugate roots, and a check in the original or equivalent equation. Complex-coefficient quadratics are not added to this standard's scope.

reviews.coverageReason: Added general explanations of rational closure and the two mixed rational/irrational claims. Existing classification and arithmetic topics permit computing or identifying examples, but do not explicitly justify these universal statements. The general defined-operation topic addresses closure and laws on a specified set, but does not supply rational fraction representations or the mixed-input irrationality arguments. The new topic explicitly develops integer-fraction representations, rational additive inverses, and reciprocals of nonzero rationals before using reverse arithmetic. It makes the nonzero rational multiplier essential and does not claim that irrational numbers are closed under arithmetic.

sources.note: N-RN.B.3 asks for explanations of all four claims, including the nonzero condition on the rational factor of an irrational number.

Task 1817 proves closure using integer fractions and proves the mixed-input claims by reversing the arithmetic. Its commentary explains why nonrepeating-decimal identification alone is unhelpful for these proofs.
Number Progression, printed page 17, distinguishes the closure of rational numbers from the failure of closure for irrationals and connects these explanations to mathematical argument.

alignments.reason: Explains each native closure or mixed-input irrationality statement with general arguments, and also requires interpreting the zero-factor exception and avoiding false extensions to two irrational inputs.
